expected_answer.conclusion: The complete displayed 4×11 cohort is finite. Population-standardized PCA retains 86.95% of variance in two components, and independent score-covariance eigenvalues agree with PCA explained variances within the requested tolerances. Seed-42 k-means separates CC(=O)N from the other three molecules. This is interpretable descriptively but not validated; four-decimal descriptor exposure prevents claims about full native precision or robust grouping under hidden rounding.

clustering.method: Euclidean k-means on the actual two-PC scores, two groups, ten initializations, seed 42

analysis.descriptor_columns: EState-VSA bins 1 through 11, in native order

independent_score_covariance.arithmetic_precision: Off-diagonal cancellation is reported as zero at this arithmetic resolution; the eigentool received the explicitly constructed covariance rounded to 12 decimals.
independent_score_covariance.comparison: Reverse the eigenvalue order to compare with descending PCA explained variances. Absolute differences are approximately 3.70e-13 and 7.99e-14, respectively, satisfying |difference| <= 1e-8 + 1e-6*|PCA variance|. PCA sign changes do not change these eigenvalues.
independent_score_covariance.definition: Center the four score rows and sum outer products, dividing by n−1 = 3.

analysis.precision: The complete eleven-bin vectors were obtained, but the descriptor tool exposes only four decimal places. All exposed digits were preserved; unrounded native values are unavailable. Subsequent fitted arrays were transferred through exact observation bindings.

rounding_comparison.comparison_scope: The covariance/PCA agreement is an internal numerical check on the same displayed data. Four-decimal native rounding is generally larger than the supplied descriptor-level tolerance; it does not establish agreement with unavailable unrounded vectors. No absolute unit convention is asserted.
rounding_comparison.conditional_covariance_bound: If bins 1, 6 and 11 are genuinely structural zeros, the standardized matrix perturbation has Frobenius norm below 0.00051. The corresponding full standardized sample-covariance perturbation has norm below approximately 0.00193, also bounding its ordered eigenvalue changes. This is a conservative propagated-rounding bound, not an observed discrepancy or a clustering-stability test.
rounding_comparison.native_display_uncertainty: For ordinary nearest rounding to four decimals, each displayed descriptor has uncertainty up to 0.00005. This uncertainty applies to unavailable native values, not to the exact stored displayed matrix used for fitting.
rounding_comparison.propagation: A column mean can differ by at most 0.00005, and its population standard deviation by at most 0.00005. For each nonconstant displayed column, a standardized entry has error bounded by (0.0001 + |z|*0.00005)/(scale−0.00005). Using the observed minimum nonconstant scale and maximum |z| gives a conservative bound below 0.00009 per entry.

standardization.definition: Per-column cohort mean and population standard deviation (denominator 4); scale 1 for constant columns.

decision.descriptive_grouping: M1 is isolated from M0, M2 and M3. Its bins 2, 5, 8 and 10 are nonzero where the other displayed rows are zero; these standardized coordinates have equal PC1 loadings. This makes the partition descriptively understandable within this panel, not validated beyond it.
decision.native_precision_requirement: Only partially satisfiable: full bin coverage is available, but full unrounded native precision is not exposed by the supplied descriptor tool.
decision.numerical_reconciliation: Passed for the displayed-data analysis at rtol=1e-6 and atol=1e-8.

limitations: Only four molecules were analyzed; the standardized centered data have rank at most three, and the two retained components omit about 13.05% of variance.

Standardization gives each nonconstant bin equal marginal variance. Several bins encode the same singleton pattern here, so correlated coordinates can amplify that pattern in PCA and Euclidean clustering.

Displayed zero-variance columns are not proof of exact native zero variance. If rounded zeros conceal tiny variation, standardization can amplify it substantially; the conditional rounding bound would not apply to those columns.
No perturbation experiment established stability of the PC directions or cluster memberships under native rounding. Component signs and cluster labels are arbitrary.
The groups are a descriptive teaching-panel result, not established chemical classes. No experimental, predictive, external or out-of-sample validation is established.

question: EState-VSA descriptor cohort. Obtain the full native descriptor vector for each of the four supplied molecules in declared order. Construct the complete four-row numeric feature matrix; report its dimension and any non-finite entries. Fit per-coordinate population standardization to this descriptive cohort, with scale one for constant columns, then project to two principal components and cluster the actual scores into two groups with seed42. Independently construct the sample covariance of those two scores and obtain its symmetric eigenvalues; reconcile them with the two PCA explained variances, allowing sign/label ambiguity. Report retained variance, membership by molecule, zero-variance columns and whether grouping is interpretable on only four objects. All eleven native bins are printed to four decimals. Compare the displayed vectors with propagated rounding; do not invent absolute unit conventions. Use only actual successful observations, preserve sample identity and complete vector precision, and report the numerical intermediates, comparison and limitations. No experimental or predictive validation is established by this descriptive teaching panel.

workflow_goal: EState-VSA descriptor cohort: Obtain the full native descriptor vector for each of the four supplied molecules in declared order. Construct the complete four-row numeric feature matrix; report its dimension and any non-finite entries. Fit per-coordinate population standardization to this descriptive cohort, with scale one for constant columns, then project to two principal components and cluster the actual scores into two groups with seed42. Independently construct the sample covariance of those two scores and obtain its symmetric eigenvalues; reconcile them with the two PCA explained variances, allowing sign/label ambiguity. Report retained variance, membership by molecule, zero-variance columns and whether grouping is interpretable on only four objects. All eleven native bins are printed to four decimals. Compare the displayed vectors with propagated rounding; do not invent absolute unit conventions.

expected_answer.conclusion: For the available four-decimal 4-by-11 descriptor matrix, population standardization followed by two-component PCA retains 79.203% of variance. Seed-42 k-means groups M0 with M1 and M2 with M3. Independently assembled sample score covariance has eigenvalues matching the PCA variances within the supplied tolerances. This is a descriptive teaching-panel result, not a validated chemical classification or predictive finding.

analysis.descriptor_columns: EState_VSA1 through EState_VSA11, in native order

independent_score_covariance_check.comparison: Reversing eigenvalue order matches the descending PCA explained variances. Absolute discrepancies are approximately 1.66e-11 and 3.95e-11, respectively, well within atol + rtol*abs(reference), with atol=1e-8 and rtol=1e-6. The population-standardized descriptors have sample variance 4/3 per nonconstant column; score covariance must likewise use denominator 3, not 4.
independent_score_covariance_check.construction: Center the four observed score rows by their column means, then compute C_ab = sum_i[(t_ia - mean_a)(t_ib - mean_b)]/3. Direct score-product sums give the following covariance, rounded to ten decimal places; the cross-covariance rounds to zero.

analysis.precision: All eleven bins were obtained for every molecule. The descriptor tool exposes only four-decimal strings, not its underlying unrounded values. The matrix preserves every available decimal; this analysis therefore concerns the displayed vectors, not inaccessible full-precision descriptors. No absolute unit convention is asserted.

rounding_comparison.descriptor_uncertainty: Ordinary four-decimal rounding gives at most 0.00005 absolute error per displayed coordinate. Comparing two independently rounded coordinates propagates this to at most 0.0001 error in their difference. Every molecule pair differs in at least one coordinate by far more than this bound, so no displayed pair is rounding-indistinguishable.
rounding_comparison.scope: These bounds do not constitute a measured unrounded PCA or clustering sensitivity analysis. Constant printed columns cannot reveal hidden sub-rounding variation.
rounding_comparison.standardization_propagation: For a nonconstant column with rounding bound epsilon=0.00005, mean error and population-scale error are each bounded by epsilon. Consequently, standardized-coordinate error is bounded by epsilon*(2+abs(z))/(scale-epsilon). Across the observed nonconstant columns, a conservative bound is approximately 0.0000722, conditional on the displayed constant columns remaining constant in the unrounded data.
rounding_comparison.tolerance_interpretation: The requested numerical tolerance is appropriate for comparing the covariance eigenvalues with PCA variances from the same displayed-data pipeline. It does not establish agreement with unavailable unrounded descriptors: even at the largest displayed coordinate, 25.6711, atol + rtol*abs(x) is about 0.00002568, smaller than the possible 0.00005 printing error.

standardization.definition: Fit on all four descriptive-cohort rows: z_ij = (x_ij - mean_j)/scale_j, using population standard deviation and scale 1 for constant columns.

decision.clustering_method: Euclidean k-means on the actual two-PC scores, two clusters, seed 42, ten initializations.
decision.interpretation: The partition is descriptively interpretable as separation primarily along PC1: M0/M1 have positive scores and M2/M3 negative scores. It is not evidence of stable chemical classes. The two members of the second group are substantially separated along PC2. PCA axis signs and cluster label numbers are arbitrary; consistent sign flips or label permutations do not alter the partition or variance reconciliation.

limitations: Only four objects are present. Centered data have rank at most three, so these fitted directions and groups are highly cohort-dependent.
Standardization weights each nonconstant coordinate equally. Bins 6 and 7 have identical standardized profiles in this panel, so correlated descriptor information receives repeated weight.
Two-component projection discards about 20.8% of standardized sample variance; clustering in that projection need not equal clustering in the complete descriptor space.
Only displayed four-decimal descriptors were available. Exact unrounded native vectors and their downstream sensitivity cannot be recovered from these observations.
No resampling, external cohort, experimental validation, predictive validation, or generalizable grouping has been established.

question: EState-VSA descriptor cohort. Obtain the full native descriptor vector for each of the four supplied molecules in declared order. Construct the complete four-row numeric feature matrix; report its dimension and any non-finite entries. Fit per-coordinate population standardization to this descriptive cohort, with scale one for constant columns, then project to two principal components and cluster the actual scores into two groups with seed42. Independently construct the sample covariance of those two scores and obtain its symmetric eigenvalues; reconcile them with the two PCA explained variances, allowing sign/label ambiguity. Report retained variance, membership by molecule, zero-variance columns and whether grouping is interpretable on only four objects. All eleven native bins are printed to four decimals. Compare the displayed vectors with propagated rounding; do not invent absolute unit conventions. Use only actual successful observations, preserve sample identity and complete vector precision, and report the numerical intermediates, comparison and limitations. No experimental or predictive validation is established by this descriptive teaching panel.

hydrogen_reconciliation.bond_reconciliation: The original CCCO chain has 3 heavy-atom bonds. Adding 8 explicit hydrogen bonds yields 11 bonds, matching both outputs.
hydrogen_reconciliation.calculation: 12 total atoms - 4 heavy atoms = 8 hydrogen atoms; C3H8O contains 3 carbon atoms, 1 oxygen atom and 8 hydrogen atoms.
hydrogen_reconciliation.interpretation: The returned SMILES writes all eight hydrogens explicitly, whereas CCCO leaves them implicit. This representation change does not change molecular identity.

results.decision: Both connectivity recovery and bond-order assignment preserve the original input's standard InChI identity. No recovery-induced identity failure was observed, and neither returned graph was substituted with the starting graph.
limitations: Both tools internally add hydrogens and embed a conformer from the same input graph with seed 42. This is an internal consistency comparison, not independent experimental structure elucidation.

dimensional_analysis.gravimetric: 1 mAh/g = (10^-3 Ah)/(10^-3 kg) = 1 Ah/kg. Thus energy[Wh/kg] = voltage[V] × capacity[mAh/g].
dimensional_analysis.volumetric: 1 mAh/cm³ = (10^-3 Ah)/(10^-3 L) = 1 Ah/L. Thus V × capacity[mAh/cm³] has the same numerical value as energy[Wh/L]; the correct factor is 1, not 1000.

implied_electrode_mass_density.interpretation: Both denominators are finite and nonzero, so both routes are defined. The two negative energies yield a positive density ratio. This is an implied normalization density, not an independently measured bulk or packed-electrode density.

dimensional_analysis.gravimetric: V × mAh/g = mWh/g = Wh/kg. The correct numerical factor is also 1.
dimensional_analysis.volumetric: V × mAh/cm^3 = mWh/cm^3 = Wh/L: the 10^-3 charge conversion cancels the 10^3 volume conversion. The correct numerical factor is 1, not 1000.

implied_density.interpretation: All four capacity/energy inputs are finite and nonzero, so both ratios are defined. Their agreement implies the same normalization mass density; it does not independently establish a measured bulk electrode density.

workflow_goal: Compare analogue ranking from complete native MACCS bit vectors, sparse atom-pair bit sets and topological-torsion count fingerprints for the query and two candidates. Use binary Jaccard/Tanimoto for bit sets and generalized count Tanimoto c*d/(c*c+d*d-c*d) for sparse count vectors, over the union of keys. Report the exact encodings, intersections/norms, both query-candidate scores per method, ties or undefined empty-set cases and whether the preferred analogue changes with encoding. Obtain native strict rotatable-bond counts for the three graphs to contextualize torsion-fingerprint differences; counts are not a substitute for the actual fingerprints. Do not compare bit positions across methods or claim validated chemical activity.

expected_answer.conclusion: Candidate_A is the preferred analogue under MACCS, atom-pair bit-set, and topological-torsion count Tanimoto. Encoding changes the score separation but not the winner. Matching rotatable-bond counts do not imply matching torsion fingerprints, and these structural comparisons do not establish chemical activity.

comparisons.formula: dot(Q,C) / (dot(Q,Q) + dot(C,C) - dot(Q,C)), evaluated over the union of keys

analysis.encoding_notes: The complete native MACCS outputs preserve all 167 entries, including the zero at index 0 and native floating-point display. On-bit indices provide an additional lossless binary representation: every unlisted index is zero. Atom-pair lists preserve every returned on-bit entry in native order. Torsion dictionaries preserve every returned key and integer multiplicity in native order; unlisted keys have count zero. No returned fingerprint entries are missing or truncated.
analysis.tolerance_assessment: Neither exact equality nor a comparison using atol=1e-8 and rtol=1e-6 yields a tie for any method. All comparison denominators are positive; no empty-set convention is needed.
analysis.torsion_context: Native strict rotatable-bond counts are 1, 2, 1 in panel order. Candidate_A shares two torsion keys with the query despite having an additional rotatable bond. Candidate_B has the same rotatable-bond count as the query but no shared torsion keys. Its count of 2 at key 5662327328 contributes 4 to its squared norm. Thus rotatable-bond counts neither determine torsion identities nor replace multiplicity-sensitive fingerprints.

decision.interpretation: Candidate_A ranks first under all three encodings. Ranking confidence from score separation is encoding-sensitive: the atom-pair margin is only 1/120, whereas MACCS and torsion comparisons separate the candidates more strongly. These margins are descriptive within each method, not calibrated confidence estimates.

limitations: Only the supplied three molecular graphs and native tool outputs were evaluated; no experimental activity, target binding, or validated analogue performance was measured.
Bit positions and torsion keys were compared only within their own encoding. Scores across different fingerprint methods are not interchangeable measures of chemical or biological similarity.
The atom-pair comparison uses the returned SparseBitVect on-bit sets, not an atom-pair count fingerprint. The torsion comparison retains counts, including candidate_B's multiplicity of 2.
Native MACCS values were returned as formatted floating-point zeros and ones; complete outputs are retained rather than replaced by rounded or truncated vectors.
All requested fingerprint entries and rotatable-bond counts were returned without apparent truncation. Toolkit version metadata was not supplied.

expected_answer.conclusion: The preferred analogue changes with encoding: MACCS and atom-pair binary Tanimoto favor candidate_A, while topological-torsion count Tanimoto favors candidate_B. There are no ties, undefined comparisons, or observed missing fingerprint entries. Native rotatable-bond counts are 0, 0, and 2 in panel order, but the ranking reversal is established by the actual fingerprints, not those counts.

MACCS.encoding: Native 167-position binary vectors, including position 0. The zero-based on-bit lists below are a lossless compact representation: every other position is zero.

atom_pair.encoding: Native SparseBitVect on-bit sets; absent positions are off. No count weighting or cross-method bit alignment is used.

analysis.encoding_completeness: All three MACCS outputs contain complete 167-entry vectors without ellipses. All returned atom-pair on-bit lists and torsion nonzero-count dictionaries are complete. No missing or truncated entries were observed. Native-output references below preserve the returned entries and formatting, including MACCS values printed as 0. and 1.
analysis.interpretation: Candidate_A contains every query MACCS on-bit and every query atom-pair on-bit, so both binary encodings favor A. Torsion counts instead favor B: its three shared query keys each retain count 2, giving dot product 12, whereas A's three shared keys give dot product 8. The native rotatable-bond counts contextualize B's greater flexibility, but torsion fingerprints also encode ring paths: query and A have nonempty, distinct torsion fingerprints despite both having zero rotatable bonds. Thus rotatable-bond counts cannot replace the observed fingerprints.

decision.shortlist_recommendation: There is no encoding-independent winner. Prefer A under either requested binary fingerprint comparison; prefer B under the requested torsion-count comparison. Retain both if the shortlist must remain robust to encoding choice.
decision.ties: None; the score differences exceed the supplied rtol=1e-6 and atol=1e-8.
decision.undefined_cases: None: all binary unions and count-Tanimoto denominators are positive.

limitations: These are within-method fingerprint similarities, not validated chemical activity, potency, safety, or experimental analogue performance.
Bit positions and torsion identifiers were compared only within their respective methods; equal numeric identifiers across methods have no asserted relationship.
The native rotatable-bond tool calls CalcNumRotatableBonds with its default behavior; it does not expose an explicit strictness argument or toolkit version.
Native fingerprint defaults and toolkit version were not independently varied or validated. Different encodings can emphasize different structural features.
Decimal scores are approximations; the reported fractions and integer intersections, dot products, and squared norms specify the calculations exactly.

Do not compare bit positions across methods or claim validated chemical activity.

question: Shape-only versus atom-type-conditioned conformer grouping. Compare shape-only12-coordinate Ultrafast Shape Recognition (USR) with60-coordinate atom-type-conditioned USRCAT on the same four supplied molecules under hydrogen-added seed42 computational conformers. For each encoding separately preserve every native descriptor coordinate and molecule order, fit cohort population standardization with scaleone for constant columns, project to two PCs and cluster the actual scores into two groups with seed42. Reconcile the sample covariance eigenvalues of each two-dimensional score matrix with its PCA explained variances. Report both full native feature matrices, constant coordinates, retained variance, memberships, centroids and cross-encoding pair co-membership changes. Do not compare encoded coordinate positions, inertias or component signs as if physically commensurate. Explain whether including atom-type-conditioned shape information changes the observed descriptive partition; four molecules establish no generalization or measured geometry.

question: Phonon branch-count and stability-evidence sufficiency. Assess whether the accessible published DFPT phonon report supports a soft-mode claim for the supplied material. Obtain its phonon-structure composition/site count, branch and q-point counts and compare them with the separate summary composition/site count, retaining distinct lattice/cell provenance. Check branches=3N using the phonon cell. Identify precisely which frequency range is a DOS sampling axis and whether actual mode eigenfrequencies are exposed as readable values or only saved artifact filenames. If actual mode values are unavailable through the supplied interfaces, state that the threshold test is undetermined and specify the missing evidence; do not read local files outside tool access, infer a mode minimum from the DOS grid, or invent an instability conclusion. Report explicit source URLs/hashes actually returned and do not claim experimental or full-Brillouin-zone stability. The supplied soft-mode threshold is only to be tested when actual band-mode values are accessible. Numerical agreement uses rtol=1e-6 and atol=1e-8 with propagated source display rounding.

expected_answer.conclusion: The phonon cell and separate summaries agree on GaAs with two sites, and the reported six branches satisfy branches = 3N. Actual mode eigenfrequencies are not exposed through the supplied interfaces, so the -0.2 THz soft-mode threshold test remains undetermined. comparison.rounding_treatment: Reported compositions and integer site/branch counts agree exactly at their displayed precision; no discrepancy depends on display rounding. There is no separate summary lattice available for a numerical lattice comparison.

frequency_evidence.access_assessment: The report exposes counts, a DOS-axis range, structure and provenance, but only filenames for the full saved arrays. No supplied interface provides file-reading access to those artifacts.
frequency_evidence.range_interpretation: The returned frequency_range describes the DOS frequency sampling axis, not the minimum and maximum band-mode eigenfrequencies. Its negative lower endpoint is not evidence of a negative mode.

decision.meaning: The accessible report is insufficient to establish or exclude a mode below the supplied threshold; the threshold was not tested against the DOS axis.
decision.missing_evidence: Readable actual band-mode eigenfrequencies in THz, indexed by branch and sampled q-point, with their numerical precision and q-point/path provenance, are required to compute the sampled mode minimum and compare it with -0.2 THz.

limitations: No local artifact files were read, and no mode minimum was inferred from the DOS sampling grid.
Six branches for a two-site phonon cell establish branch-count consistency, not dynamical stability.
The published DFPT report is computational evidence, not experimental validation or a new phonon calculation.
Even readable eigenfrequencies at the reported 145 q-points would not by themselves establish full-Brillouin-zone stability.

expected_answer.conclusion: Audit of the supplied RefSeq coding sequence for human INS (source accession NM_000207.3, input region CDS 60..392, used here as local coordinates 1..333 of the supplied sequence only). (1) The supplied sequence is 333 nucleotides long. (2) Its GC content is 64.56456456456456 percent (215 G+C of 333 nt), as returned by NucleicAcidGCCalculator in default whole-sequence mode (window_size=0, base_type=DNA). (3) Exactly one translational reading frame of the supplied sequence contains an open reading frame of at least 30 codons: reading frame 1 of the direct (sense) strand, whose ORF extends from base 1 to base 333, i.e. the entire 333 bp sequence = 111 codons (110 sense codons plus the terminal stop). A confirmatory ORF search on the reverse complement returned two additional >=30-codon ORFs in that reverse-complement sequence's own frame 1 (reverse-complement bases 1..213 = 71 codons, and reverse-complement bases 238..333 = 32 codons); these are antisense-strand ORFs of the supplied CDS and are not the gene's coding ORF, so the frame carrying the INS ORF is frame 1 of the supplied sequence. (4) Translation of the full supplied coding sequence in frame 1 is MALWMRLLPLLALLALWGPDPAAAFVNQHLCGSHLVEALYLVCGERGFFYTPKTRREAEDLQVGQVELGGGPGAGSLQPLALEGSLQKRGIVEQCCTSICSLYQLENYCN*. (5) Yes: the translation starts with methionine (M, from the ATG initiator at bases 1-3) and ends with a stop codon (the terminal TAA at bases 331-333, rendered as *). CpG caller: CpGIslandPrediction (Gardiner-Garden and Frommer 1987; 200 bp window, 1 bp shift; Obs/Exp > 0.6 and GC > 50%) reports 'No CpG island regions were identified', i.e. 0 CpG islands in this 333 bp sequence. These results apply only to this supplied NM_000207.3 CDS sequence and are not generalised to other transcripts.

A trypsin digest at zero missed cleavages (cleavage C-terminal to K/R) yields 4 peptides: HSQGTFTSDYSK, YLDSR, R and AQDFVQWLMNT. The two longest are HSQGTFTSDYSK (12 residues, neutral monoisotopic mass 1356.5946 Da) and AQDFVQWLMNT (11 residues, neutral monoisotopic mass 1351.6231 Da). Every peptide mass is a neutral, free-termini, monoisotopic mass in daltons; the intact molecular weight is an average mass in daltons; the TPSA unit is Angstrom^2 and the pI is unitless.

The two coefficient sets are nearly identical because raw x spans 0.1 to 998.5 (variance of order 1e5), so an L2 penalty of 1.0 is negligible relative to the data's scale. Held-out predictions: OLS = [10.273152458295868, 117.45327927562589, 228.52542187123885, 667.1256615008156, 448.3744157060415, 0.29362482167296244], ridge = [10.2732728005222, 117.45337053511743, 228.52548299191864, 667.1256036097454, 448.3744171719124, 0.29374787178893813]. On the raw scale the ridge model has the marginally lower held-out RMSE (1.0060028878998661 vs 1.006024400611715). (B) TRAINING-STANDARDIZED PREDICTOR SCALE: the standardizer, fit on the training rows only (fit_basis 'training_features only'), returned mean 454.61333333333334 and population scale 350.49257788939775; those parameters were then applied to all 36 rows, so the held-out rows were transformed but never used to compute the parameters. OLS on the standardized training column returns slope 349.77503674784526 and intercept 453.7766666666667, with training MSE 0.705456932401727; ridge (alpha=1, unpenalized intercept) on the same standardized column returns slope 338.4919710463017 and intercept 453.7766666666667, with training MSE 128.01302855774927. Here the penalty bites hard: it shrinks the standardized slope by 338.4919710463017/349.77503674784526 = 0.9678 of its unpenalized value. Held-out standardized-OLS metrics: MAE 0.8424073943849478, RMSE 1.006024400611716, R-squared 0.9999827593057737. Held-out standardized-ridge metrics: MAE 8.950620268455031, RMSE 10.097521870487704, R-squared 0.9982631299533702. On the standardized scale the OLS model clearly has the lower held-out RMSE (1.006024400611716 vs 10.097521870487704). The held-out ranking therefore changes between the two scales: ridge wins (barely) on the raw predictor, OLS wins by a wide margin on the training-standardized predictor. The reason is that an L2 penalty is not scale invariant. Ridge penalizes the squared coefficient magnitude, and a coefficient's magnitude depends on the units of its feature. On the raw scale one unit of slope moves the prediction by one y-unit per x-unit; because x has a variance of about 1.23e5, the penalty term alpha=1 is minuscule next to the residual curvature of the likelihood (equivalently, an effective penalty of ~8.1e-6 in standardized units), so the raw ridge fit is numerically almost the OLS fit and the two held-out metric sets differ only in the seventh decimal place. After training-only standardization each feature has unit variance, so a slope of ~350 is the natural size and alpha=1 is a genuinely binding penalty: it shrinks the slope to 338.49, adding a systematic bias that shows up mainly where the training data are sparse, i.e. at the smallest held-out x values, where the fitted intercept dominates and the shrunken slope underestimates the response (held-out row 1 predicted 24.58 vs observed 11.1, and row 6 predicted 14.92 vs observed 0.5). That bias inflates the standardized-ridge held-out MAE/RMSE by roughly a factor of ten.

expected_answer.conclusion: Ridge regression (alpha=1.0) with shuffled 5-fold cross-validation and seed 42 was applied to the 36-observation calibration dataset (x = predictor, y = response). CrossValidateRegressor returned per-fold held-out RMSE values of 11.8694, 11.1107, 11.4915, 11.4800 and 16.3301 (MAE 10.5944, 9.5803, 10.6853, 10.6774, 14.7085), giving a mean cross-validated RMSE of 12.4563 and mean MAE of 11.2492. Standardization inside the cross-validation was fitted on each training fold only (preprocessing_fit_basis = 'each training fold only'), so no information from the held-out fold leaks into the scaler. A single ridge model with the same penalty (alpha=1.0) fitted on the first 30 supplied rows returned coefficients [0.9979524928733262] with intercept 0.09415737321427287 and a training MSE of 0.705457; applied to the last 6 rows it predicted [10.2733, 117.4534, 228.5255, 667.1256, 448.3744, 0.2937], and RegressionMetrics on those 6 held-out rows returned RMSE 1.0060, MAE 0.8424, MSE 1.0120 and R^2 0.999983. The cross-validated mean RMSE (12.4563) and the single-split RMSE (1.0060) therefore do NOT agree within 0.1; their absolute difference is 11.4503, which is far larger than the 0.1 tolerance, so the two error estimates are not in agreement. The large discrepancy is expected: the shuffled folds are dominated by the eight near-zero x,y observations, whose tiny magnitudes make the per-fold RMSE small only when they are concentrated in the training set, while the single split keeps that cluster entirely in training and holds out only large-magnitude rows, whose absolute errors are comparatively small relative to their scale.

NAD+ has InChIKey BAWFJGJZGIEFAR-NNYOXOHSSA-N with formula C21H27N7O14P2 and TPSA 321.09 A^2; NADH has InChIKey BOPGDPNILDQYTO-NNYOXOHSSA-N with formula C21H29N7O14P2 and TPSA 317.62 A^2. The formula difference, derived by arithmetic on the two returned formulas, is 2 H (NADH = NAD+ + H2). The structural change visible in the returned structures is in the nicotinamide (pyridinium) ring and its attached phosphate: in the NAD+ structure the ring is written as an aromatic pyridinium with a positively charged ring nitrogen ([n+]) and the pyrophosphate carries a deprotonated oxygen ([O-]), whereas in the NADH structure the same ring is written as a non-aromatic dihydropyridine with a neutral trivalent ring nitrogen (N) in the SMILES ring sequence C1=CN(...)C=CC1 and both phosphate groups are written fully protonated (OP(=O)(O)O). The returned InChI hydrogen-layer strings also differ correspondingly, and both keys share the same second block (NNYOXOHSSA) and the same /t.../m1/s1 stereo layer. No metabolic or therapeutic behaviour is asserted.

expected_answer.conclusion: Registry-independent identifiers were derived for the glutathione redox pair. PubChem name lookup returned glutathione (CAS-free name query) as CID 124886 with canonical SMILES N[C@@H](CCC(=O)N[C@@H](CS)C(=O)NCC(=O)O)C(=O)O, and glutathione disulfide as CID 65359 with canonical SMILES N[C@@H](CCC(=O)N[C@@H](CSSC[C@H](NC(=O)CC[C@H](N)C(=O)O)C(=O)NCC(=O)O)C(=O)NCC(=O)O)C(=O)O. Converting each returned structure to InChI and then to an InChIKey gave glutathione InChIKey RWSXRVCMGQZWBV-WDSKDSINSA-N (from InChI=1S/C10H17N3O6S/...) and glutathione disulfide InChIKey YPZRWBKMTBYPTK-BJDJZHNGSA-N (from InChI=1S/C20H32N6O12S2/...). The tools returned molecular formula C10H17N3O6S with TPSA 158.82 (unit: square angstroms, A^2) for glutathione, and C20H32N6O12S2 with TPSA 317.64 A^2 for glutathione disulfide. The formula difference (derived by arithmetic on the two returned formulas, not a tool-returned value) is C10H15N3O6S, i.e. glutathione disulfide minus glutathione equals +C10 +H15 +N3 +O6 +S1. The 15-hydrogen difference corresponds to 15 electrons' worth of hydrogen atoms (a 15 H atom / 15 electron difference), since each hydrogen atom carries one electron; this is a whole-number arithmetic statement about the formulas. Structurally, the only difference visible in the two returned structures is that glutathione disulfide contains an additional -CH2-S-S-CH2- linkage joining the two gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine units, whereas the returned glutathione structure contains a free thiol (-SH, the C4-20 atom/hydrogen in its InChI hydrogen layer); the two monomer units in the returned disulfide structure are otherwise the same connectivity with the same 4 stereocentres (t9-,10-,11-,12-/m0/s1 versus t5-,6-/m0/s1). No antioxidant, redox-catalytic, or therapeutic behaviour is claimed; the redox pairing is only the structural (disulfide/thiol) relationship visible in the returned structures.

Held-out predictions (last 6 rows, order preserved: x = 10.2, 117.6, 228.9, 668.4, 449.2, 0.2) are OLS: [10.2731524583, 117.4532792756, 228.5254218712, 667.1256615008, 448.3744157060, 0.2936248217] and ridge: [10.3934620719, 117.5445140358, 228.5865259873, 667.0677861192, 448.3758811797, 0.4166415911]. Held-out RMSE is 1.0060244006 for OLS and 0.9880829646 for ridge, with R-squared 0.9999827593 (OLS) and 0.9999833688 (ridge). Ridge therefore has the lower held-out RMSE, by 1.0060244006 - 0.9880829646 = 0.0179414360 (about 1.78% relative). On the training rows, MSE is 0.7054569324 for OLS and 0.7144598682 for ridge, so the fit with the lower held-out RMSE (ridge) does NOT have the lower training MSE; OLS fits the training data slightly better. This is the classic bias-variance pattern: the alpha=1000 penalty shrinks the slope away from the OLS value, accepting a marginally worse in-sample fit (higher training MSE) in exchange for slightly better generalization to the held-out rows (lower held-out RMSE). On this dataset the effect is tiny - both models are essentially the same near-perfect line, both explain about 99.998% of held-out variance, and the ridge advantage in held-out RMSE is only ~0.018 on a y-scale of ~0-1000, so the penalty buys a very small robustness gain rather than a qualitatively better model.

expected_answer.conclusion: Two runs of the identical median-threshold logistic pipeline were executed on the 36-row Norris calibration set. The classification rule was y >= that run's training-response median, computed only on that run's training rows. Run 1 (split A: first 30 rows train, last 6 rows held out) has threshold 448.05 (median of y[1..30], observation o001), giving 15 positives / 15 negatives in training. Its standardized L2 logistic model (o004) reports mean=454.6133, scale=350.4926, coefficient=2.3202, intercept=0.03484, training accuracy 0.9667. On the 6 held-out rows (30-35, truth labels [0,0,0,1,1,0]; labels from the run's own threshold) it predicts [0,0,0,1,0,0] (o006): the row (x=449.2, y=448.9) is a false negative, so its confusion matrix is TN=4, FP=0, FN=1, TP=1 (o008), accuracy 0.8333 and macro F1 0.7778. Run 2 (split B: first 32 rows train, last 4 rows held out) has threshold 393.3 (median of y[1..32], observation o002), giving 16 positives / 16 negatives. Its model (o005) reports mean=430.1938, scale=352.5510, coefficient=2.4108, intercept=0.11630, training accuracy 1.0. On the 4 held-out rows (32-35, truth labels [0,1,1,0]) it predicts [0,1,1,0] (o007), so the confusion matrix is TN=2, FP=0, FN=0, TP=2 (o009), accuracy 1.0 and macro F1 1.0. The split-B (32 training rows / 4 held-out rows) run therefore gives the higher held-out accuracy (1.0 vs 0.8333); the gain comes from the shifted-threshold relabeling, since shifting the split lowers the run's training median to 393.3, a cut that lies inside the empty gap between the low-response cluster (y <= 339.1) and the high-response cluster (y >= 447.5) and so is perfectly separable in x, whereas the 448.05 cut makes the borderline row (y=447.5) a negative while the adjacent cluster value y=448.9 is a positive. In each run no held-out response entered that run's threshold or that run's fit: Run 1 thresholds/fits used only rows 1-30 and its six held-out responses (rows 31-36) never touched the median 448.05 or the scaler/logistic fit; Run 2 used only rows 1-32 for both the median 393.3 and the fit, with its four held-out responses (rows 33-36) excluded. The standardization reported by each fitted model is authoritative and was applied unchanged at prediction time; no scaler was refitted on any held-out data.

expected_answer.conclusion: Audit of the supplied 333 bp linear DNA sequence (Human insulin INS coding sequence; base composition A=57, C=106, G=109, T=61). SummaryEnzymeCleavageSites was given the sequence and the topology in the documented combined form '<sequence>.linear' and echoed the topology as linear ("Results for linear 333 residue sequence "sequence" starting "ATGGCCCTGT""), so the audited sequence length is 333 bp and the echoed topology is linear. Its Markdown site table lists 113 enzymes in total, of which 12 report a position that is not none: AfaI (gt|ac) 289; AluI (ag|ct) 113, 202, 313; ApaI (gggcc|c) 215; BfaI (c|tag) 122, 331; HaeIII (gg|cc) 5, 44, 213, 242; HpaII (c|cgg) 166; MspI (c|cgg) 166; PhoI (gg|cc) 5, 44, 213, 242; PstI (ctgca|g) 186, 234, 261; PvuII (cag|ctg) 313; RsaI (gt|ac) 289; SbfI (cctgca|gg) 186. The largest number of positions reported by any single enzyme is 4 (reported by HaeIII and by PhoI); the remaining ten enzymes report 1-3 positions each. Every reported position is a 1-based coordinate on the supplied linear sequence: each listed number falls inside the corresponding recognition-site match on the sequence (e.g. HaeIII/PhoI gg|cc at 5, 44, 213, 242 corresponds to GGCC matches spanning 3-6, 42-45, 211-214 and 240-243; PstI ctgca|g at 186, 234, 261 corresponds to CTGCAG matches spanning 181-186, 229-234 and 256-261), so the coordinates are 1-based and no 0-based reading fits. NucleicAcidGCCalculator was called with the stated window size 0 and base type DNA and returned gc_percent = 64.56456456456456 with windows = [] (no sliding-window output at window size 0); this equals the whole-sequence GC content (215 GC of 333 bases = 64.56456456456456%). Because the tool was asked for the stated window size 0 it emitted no separate windowed GC value, so the windowed GC content and the whole-sequence GC content do not differ here - both are the single whole-sequence value 64.56456456456456%. The task input's base_type value "GC" is not a valid calculator base type and the first call was rejected with the verbatim ValueError "base_type must be DNA or RNA"; the successful call therefore used base_type DNA (the sequence contains only A, C, G and T, so DNA vs RNA cannot change the result).

expected_answer.conclusion: On the first 30 rows of the 36-observation calibration dataset (x predictor, y response), the polynomial least-squares fit of degree 3 returns coefficients in the tool's descending-power order [3.1485113853686944e-09, -1.628063617247087e-06, 0.9967837160278363, 0.32777175471278436] with degree 3, per-row fitted values as returned and training residual_sum_squares 18.602195128077355. The straight-line ordinary-least-squares fit returns slope 0.9979527636622907 and intercept 0.09403426894050426 with training MSE 0.7054569324017376 over 30 training rows. The polynomial fit has the smaller training error: its residual sum of squares is 18.6022 versus the line's 30 x 0.7054569 = 21.1637, i.e. smaller by 2.5615 in SSE; on the MSE scale that is 0.6200732 versus 0.7054569, smaller by 0.0853838. That does NOT imply the more flexible cubic will predict the last 6 rows better. Both fitters were estimated from the first 30 rows only, and the cubic was chosen to minimize exactly that same in-sample sum of squares; adding terms can only reduce (never increase) the training error, so a smaller training residual is expected mechanically and is not evidence about unseen rows. Whether the cubic generalizes better on the 6 held-out rows depends on whether the extra curvature captures real signal or fits noise, and that can only be settled by an out-of-sample comparison (which was not run here). Here the cubic's leading coefficients are essentially zero (3.1e-09 for x^3, -1.6e-06 for x^2) and its slope-like term 0.99678 with intercept 0.32777 is close to the line's slope 0.99795 / intercept 0.09403, so the 30-row data are near-linear and the cubic's advantage is small and largely confined to a few small-x rows; the two fits should therefore predict the last 6 rows similarly, and the small in-sample edge is not a prediction guarantee.

held_out_implication.reason: Both fits were estimated from the first 30 rows only; minimizing training residual sum of squares is what the cubic was fitted to do, so its lower in-sample error is expected and gives no evidence about the 6 unseen rows. No held-out evaluation was run.

Digesting that exact returned sequence with the trypsin rule at 0 missed cleavages gave 26 peptides; the longest is CALINMVFQMGETGVAGFTNSLR (23 residues, positions 96-119, zero-based half-open) with a neutral monoisotopic mass of 2458.18070744909 Da. Digesting the same sequence with the glutamate-specific rule (the common name 'glu-c' was mapped by the tool to its ExPASy rule key 'glutamyl endopeptidase') at 0 missed cleavages gave 9 peptides; the longest is KLFNQDVDAAVRGILRNAKLKPVYDSLDAVRRCALINMVFQMGE (44 residues, positions 64-108) with a neutral monoisotopic mass of 4976.630317329259 Da. Trypsin therefore yields more peptides: 26 versus 9, a difference of 17 peptides. This follows directly from the residue composition of the returned sequence, which contains 13 K and 13 R (26 trypsin target residues, none followed by proline) but only 8 E and 10 D (18 glutamate/glutamyl-endopeptidase target residues). The returned trypsin digest cuts at all 26 K/R sites inside the chain, producing 26 peptides (the trypsin rule is ([KR](?=[^P]))|((?<=W)K(?=P))|((?<=M)R(?=P))); the rule actually applied for the 'glutamate-specific' digest has specificity 'E' only (as shown by the tool's own 'enzyme' field '''glutamyl endopeptidase'''), so it cuts only at the 8 internal E positions (5, 11, 22, 45, 62, 64, 108, 128) and ignores the 10 D positions (10, 20, 47, 61, 70, 72, 89, 92, 127, 159, verified as intact inside e.g. LDKAIGRNCNGVITKDE and KLFNQDVDAAVRGILRNAKLKPVYDSLDAVRRCALINMVFQMGE), giving 8 cuts + 1 = 9 peptides. Because 26 cleavage-permitting residues > 8 cleavage-permitting residues in this composition, trypsin produces 17 more peptides than the Glu-C rule. All masses are reported in daltons (Da), the tool's stated mass unit, and are neutral monoisotopic masses (ion_type M, charge 0, i.e. elemental monoisotopic mass of the neutral, unmodified linear peptide with free N- and C-termini), not monoisotopic m/z and not average/monoisotopic [M+H]+ values.

Both have molecular formula C6H12O6 and TPSA 110.38 A^2. Derived comparisons from the returned values: (1) the two InChIKeys DO share their first block (both 'WQZGKKKJIJFFOK'), but their second blocks differ ('DVKNGEFBSA' vs 'VFUOTHLCSA'); (2) their molecular formulas are identical (C6H12O6 for both); (3) their polar surface areas are identical (110.38 A^2 for both). Regarding what the key comparison shows: the InChIKey is built from blocks, and the fact that the first (connectivity/skeleton) block is identical for both returned keys while the remaining stereo block differs shows that the two structures have the same constitution (same skeleton, formula and heavy-atom connectivity) but different stereochemistry - i.e. they are stereoisomers (specifically anomers), not identical compounds. The returned InChI strings corroborate this and localise it: the formula and connectivity layer (C6H12O6; c7-1-2-3(8)4(9)5(10)6(11)12-2/h2-11H,1H2) is identical in both, while the stereochemical layer differs only at the final stereocentre ('t2-,3-,4+,5-,6+/m1/s1' for alpha-D-glucose versus 't2-,3-,4+,5-,6-/m1/s1' for beta-D-glucose), i.e. at C6, the anomeric carbon carrying the OH. So the key comparison identifies the pair as stereoisomers sharing one skeleton, distinguished solely by the configuration at the anomeric centre; molecular formula and TPSA are constitution-level descriptors and therefore cannot separate the two anomers, whereas the InChIKey's stereo block does.

(1) CATH classification (PDBe CATH mappings, as returned for the single assigned domain 1ubqA00 / PDB chain A, residues 1-76): CATH ID 3.10.20.90, class 'Alpha Beta', architecture 'Roll', topology 'Ubiquitin-like (UB roll)', homologous superfamily 'Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase Catalytic Subunit; Chain A, domain 1'. (2) Chain A of 1UBQ was read from RCSB and has sequence MQIFVKTLTGKTITLEVEPSDTIENVKAKIQDKEGIPPDQQRLIFAGKQLEDGRTLSDYNIQKESTLHLVLRLRGG with length 76 residues. In-silico trypsin digestion at zero missed cleavages (Pyteomics ExPASy cleavage, neutral monoisotopic masses, free termini, no modifications) returned 12 peptides. The longest returned peptide is TITLEVEPSDTIENVK (residues 11-27, 16 residues) with neutral monoisotopic mass 1786.9200248422999 Da. (3) The molecular formula computed from that peptide's own sequence is C77H130N18O30, reported by the RDKit MolFromFASTA implementation named by the tool. The hydrogen count, 130, is consistent with an unmodified linear peptide with free N- and C-termini: the formula is built as the sum of the 16 residue formulas plus one water molecule (H = sum of residue H + 2), so it corresponds to a single linear chain with free termini and no cyclisation, dehydration or other modification. Note the formula describes the peptide TITLEVEPSDTIENVK alone (16 residues), not the whole 76-residue chain A. As an internal consistency check, the mass implied by C77H130N18O30 (1786.9200249 Da) matches the peptide mass returned by the digest tool to within 6.1e-08 Da.

expected_answer.conclusion: All three predictors were run on the 46-residue Crambin sequence (PDB 1CRN chain A). PredictProteinSolubility returned the verdict 'Prediction: Yes' (soluble). PredictTransmembraneRegion (NovoPro current ProtTM) returned ZERO transmembrane regions: the topology string is 46 consecutive 'O' characters (non-membrane/no TM helix), the only reported region is a single segment spanning residues 1-46 of type 'O', and the global label is 'SIGNAL' with probability 0.9999942779541016, i.e. the model interprets the chain as a secreted/signal-like, non-TM protein with no cleavage sites reported (cleavage_sites = []). InherentDisorderedRegionsPredictor (NovoPro current ProtIDR) labelled every one of the 46 residues as disordered (labels are all 1; per-residue prob_idr range 0.4621-0.7261 against its threshold 0.425), which corresponds to ONE contiguous disordered region covering residues 1-46. Thus the returned evidence is consistent with a soluble, non-membrane protein: the solubility tool says soluble, the transmembrane tool finds no TM segments (all-O topology, no TM-typed regions) and no signal-peptide cleavage site, and the only caveat is that the disorder tool calls the whole chain disordered rather than compactly folded. The disorder call does not contradict a soluble/non-membrane assignment, since disordered regions are non-membrane and are common in soluble proteins; it simply indicates the model expects a largely flexible chain, which for a small cysteine-rich protein such as Crambin is a plausible model artefact given that all per-residue probabilities sit only modestly above the 0.425 decision threshold. There is no evidence of membrane association in any returned value (no TM helices, no TM region count greater than zero, and a global 'SIGNAL'/secreted-type label). All of these outputs are computational predictions from the respective models, not experimental measurements, and the three tools are independent predictors that were each called once with the identical sequence.

It echoed the parsed sequence and type euk but returned degenerate single-character fields: probability of having a signal peptide = 'v', type of signal peptide = 'n', cleavage site = 'a - l' (between 'a' and 'l') and probability of the cleavage site = 'i'. These are not a usable numeric prediction: 'Invalid arguments! #100'[1], [2], [3], [4] and [5] are exactly 'n', 'v', 'a', 'l' and 'i', so the values are characters of an upstream NovoPro rejection string that the tool indexed as if it were a result row; the registered tool sends the legacy synchronous payload and this environment's NovoPro endpoint answers '[0,"Invalid arguments! #100"]'. The transmembrane tool, run on the same returned sequence, returned provider 'NovoPro current ProtTM' with global label 'SIGNAL' and global probability 0.9999933242797852, topology of 46 'O' positions, exactly 1 region (residues 1-46, type 'O', i.e. non-transmembrane/outside) and no cleavage sites - so no transmembrane helix is predicted. The amino-acid statistics returned 46 residues whose most frequent residue is a tie: C and T at 6 each (13.04%), with 36.96% aliphatic (G,A,V,L,I = 17) and 6 cysteines; every other residue is at or below 5 (A, I, P). Therefore the returned transmembrane values support rather than contradict a secreted (signal-peptide-route) assignment: the chain is predicted to carry no transmembrane segment while the current ProtTM model labels it globally 'SIGNAL' near probability 1, and the cysteine-rich, aliphatic composition is compatible with such a small hydrophobic chain (the signal-peptide tool's own probability/type fields cannot be weighed, being the error-string artifacts described above). All of these are computational predictions, not experimental determinations.

expected_answer.conclusion: Three views of the 110-residue human proinsulin sequence (UniProt P01308) were obtained, all three tools succeeding. (1) CalculateHydrophobicityAndPolarity returned hydropathy index (GRAVY) = 0.19 and estimated isoelectric point (pI) = 5.22. The tool states no unit for either value: GRAVY is a dimensionless hydropathy index and the pI is conventionally in pH units; the tool labels the pI entry as the 'polarity' proxy (it reports pI, not a separate polarity percentage). (2) ComputeProtScale returned a per-position 'Hydrophilicity Scores' table containing 102 (letter, score) rows for the 110-residue input; the returned output contains no window statement and no mean (no occurrence of 'window', 'mean' or 'average' anywhere in it), so no window size and no mean can be reported as tool-returned values. Within the returned profile the maximum score is 2.76 (rows labelled L at row 7 and A at row 8) and the minimum is -2.66 (row labelled R at row 52). (3) AminoAcidStatistics reported a 110-residue sequence; the most frequent residue is L (leucine) with count 20, i.e. 18.18% of residues (next: G 12/10.91%, A 10/9.09%). DERIVED (comparison computed from the returned values, not stated by any tool): the most frequent residue L is NOT the most hydrophobic residue on the scale as returned. The scale tool labels its output 'Hydrophilicity Scores' and is described as predicting hydrophilicity, so higher values denote more hydrophilic (less hydrophobic) residues; on that orientation L carries the profile maximum 2.76 (tied with A) and the profile minimum, i.e. the most hydrophobic entry, is R at -2.66. If instead the same returned numbers are read as a hydrophobicity scale (higher = more hydrophobic), L would be at the top, though only tied with A at 2.76 rather than uniquely; either way L is not a unique extreme of the returned profile, and the tool returns a per-position score table rather than an explicit residue ranking, so the comparison is orientation-dependent and is reported as derived. Caveat on the returned profile: its row labels are not aligned 1:1 with the input sequence - only 102 of 110 positions are scored, and for rows 2-102 the printed residue letter matches the input sequence at a +4 offset - so residue identities in that table are the tool's own labelling. A scale profile of this kind is a computed property derived from the sequence (and a chosen scale/window), not a structural measurement: no experimental or three-dimensional structural data is involved.

expected_answer.conclusion: Both rules were applied by the sequence-only tool CutPeptide to the same 110-residue input sequence with missed_cleavages=0, and both report the coordinate convention "zero-based half-open" and the method "Pyteomics ExPASy sequence cleavage rules". Under the tool-reported enzyme key "trypsin" the digestion yields 8 peptides, and under the tool-reported enzyme key "glutamyl endopeptidase" (the tool's resolution of the input "glu-c") it yields 9 peptides, so the glu-c / glutamyl endopeptidase rule yields more peptides (9 vs 8). The longest trypsin peptide is the 40-residue LLPLLALLALWGPDPAAAFVNQHLCGSHLVEALYLVCGER (coordinates 6-46) and the longest glutamyl endopeptidase peptide is the 37-residue MALWMRLLPLLALLALWGPDPAAAFVNQHLCGSHLVE (coordinates 0-37), so trypsin's longest peptide is 3 residues longer. Predicting neutral monoisotopic masses with free termini on exactly those two tool-returned peptide sequences (canonical, unmodified, linear; no missed cleavages) gives 4282.2798978434 Da for the trypsin peptide and 4066.15113260332 Da for the glutamyl endopeptidase peptide. The count difference is explained by the returned sequence itself, not by an assumption: the returned trypsin peptide set contains 7 peptide-internal cleavage positions (after R6, R46, K53, R55, R56, K88, R89), i.e. 7 cuts from 8 peptide segments, whereas the returned glutamyl endopeptidase set contains 8 such positions (after D20, E37, E45, E57, E59, D60, E67, E83, E93, E106 are the rule sites, of which the one at D20 is not realized because it is followed by P21). Reading the returned sequence directly: the 25-residue stretch from position 32 to 56, GSHLVEALYLVCGERGFFYTPKTRR, carries no K or R at all before its terminal R56, so trypsin cannot cut inside it and must return it as one long peptide (fragment 6-46 plus the adjacent 46-53, 53-55, 55-56 segments); the same stretch contains four D/E rule sites that the glutamyl endopeptidase rule does use (D34, E37, E45 and E56), which splits that region into several short peptides and is the source of the extra peptide. Conversely trypsin gains cuts that glu-c lacks around the R/K-rich segments after position 46 and after position 83 (e.g. the returned TR, R and AE / RGFFYTPKTRRE vs AE split), which is why the glutamyl rule wins by only one peptide (9 vs 8) rather than by the full site-count margin. Net effect: trypsin's longest peptide (40 aa) is longer than glu-c's longest peptide (37 aa), while glu-c returns one more peptide.

results.count_difference_explanation: Derived from the returned sequence: trypsin can only cut after K or R (not before P), and the returned 110-residue sequence supplies 7 realized K/R cut positions (R6, R46, K53, R55, R56, K88, R89), giving 8 peptides. The glutamyl endopeptidase rule cuts after D or E (not before P); the sequence has 10 such sites (D20, E37, E45, E57, E59, D60, E67, E83, E93, E106) but D20 is followed by P21 and is therefore not realized, leaving 9 cuts and 9 peptides. The decisive local feature in the returned sequence is positions 32-56 (GSHLVEALYLVCGERGFFYTPKTRR): it contains no internal K or R, so trypsin returns it as one 40-residue peptide (6-46 plus the following GFFYTPK, TR, R segments), while it contains four glu-c sites (D34, E37, E45, E56) that break the same region into short peptides; that surplus is partly offset by trypsin-only cuts among the R/K-rich segments at 46-56 and 83-93, so the final margin is one peptide (9 vs 8). The longest peptide is nevertheless longer under trypsin (40 aa) than under glu-c (37 aa).

Derived string comparisons on the returned values: the forward SMILES (o003) and the returned SMILES (o006) are NOT identical as strings (they differ in amide/imidic-acid representation and atom ordering), so the identity comparison is false at the string level even though both encode the same constitution; the fresh InChI computed from the returned structure (o008) IS identical to the original InChI from the forward SMILES (o004), so the key round-trips through a fresh InChI. The InChIKey was not recomputed from the fresh InChI in this run, so the key-level round-trip is established only indirectly: the fresh InChI equals the InChI whose key was computed as FPUZQFMQOIVPPJ-NPDAQAHQSA-N. Digesting it with the glutamyl endopeptidase / Glu-C ExPASy rule at zero missed cleavages gave 9 peptides from CutPeptide (sequence-only, Pyteomics ExPASy cleavage rules) and 9 peptides from PredictPeptideMass (mass-oriented, Pyteomics ExPASy cleavage plus elemental monoisotopic mass). Both tools reported the same rule key ('enzyme': 'glutamyl endopeptidase'), the same zero-based half-open coordinate convention ('coordinate_convention': 'zero-based half-open'), and identical start/end coordinates (0-5, 5-11, 11-22, 22-45, 45-62, 62-64, 64-108, 108-128, 128-164), so the two ordered peptide lists agree residue-for-residue (derived comparison of returned values). The mass-oriented tool's longest peptide is the 44-residue peptide at zero-based half-open coordinates [64,108), sequence KLFNQDVDAAVRGILRNAKLKPVYDSLDAVRRCALINMVFQMGE, with neutral monoisotopic mass 4976.630317329259 Da (mass type: neutral monoisotopic, free termini; unit Da). Feeding that peptide sequence to PeptideFormulaCalculator returned C219H362N64O62S3 (RDKit MolFromFASTA), which contains 64 nitrogen atoms. Deriving nitrogen from the returned sequence: the 44-residue backbone contributes one N per residue (44) and the side chains contribute more than one for several residues - Arg x4 adds 3 extra each (12 total for 16), Lys x3 adds 1 extra each, Asn x3 adds 1 extra each, Gln x2 adds 1 extra each - i.e. 44 backbone + 20 side-chain = 64 nitrogen atoms, exactly equal to the 64 N in the returned formula (derived statement). Summing the standard monoisotopic atomic masses supplied in the inputs over C219H362N64O62S3 gives 4976.630316521 Da, which agrees with the mass-oriented tool's neutral monoisotopic mass 4976.630317329259 Da to 8.1e-07 Da (derived statement).

expected_answer.conclusion: Three models were run on human proinsulin (UniProt P01308). (1) PredictProteinBinaryLocalization returned a binary localisation verdict of "Yes" (protein is predicted to localise); it reported no additional values in support of that verdict, so no score, probability or numeric support exists to quote. (2) PredictMyristoylation (IMP NMT predictor, parameter set "eukaryota without fungi and their viruses", internal_glycines enabled) returned the verdict NO: the server report states "NO myristoylation site accessible for NMT could be predicted". It reports no score and no site position, and experimental_modification_verified is false. (3) PredictProteinSolubility returned a solubility verdict of "Yes" (predicted soluble) and again provided no numeric support, only the binary label. Consistency (derived): this assessment is derived from the three returned verdicts rather than measured by any single tool. The two BioT5 verdicts, binary localisation "Yes" and solubility "Yes", are mutually consistent in being both positive calls from the same model family, while the myristoylation verdict is the dissenting one at "NO"; the three verdicts are therefore not uniformly concordant, but they are not contradictory either, since they address different properties (localisation, N-terminal myristoylation, solubility) and a negative myristoylation call is compatible with a positive localisation call: proinsulin is a secreted protein that is not N-terminally myristoylated, and its N-terminal glycine is absent (the sequence starts MALW, so the required Gly at position 2 is not present), which independently explains the NO verdict. All three outputs are model predictions computed from sequence, not experimental determinations.

question: Resolve one molecule from its registry name and carry it to a connection table, then reconcile the table against the molecule's formula. Report the canonical structure and registry identifier the name lookup returns, convert that structure to an InChI string, convert the InChI to an InChIKey, and resolve a connection table from that key through the key-to-table resolver. Report the table's counts line and its declared atom and bond counts, and report the elements present in its atom block with their counts. Separately compute the molecular formula and report whether the table's declared atom count matches the formula's heavy-atom count, labelling that reconciliation as derived, and state whether the table carries implicit or explicit hydrogens.

expected_answer.conclusion: Registry name 'nicotine' resolves (PubChem) to canonical SMILES CN1CCC[C@H]1c1cccnc1 with CID 89594. Converting that structure gives InChI=1S/C10H14N2/c1-12-7-3-5-10(12)9-4-2-6-11-8-9/h2,4,6,8,10H,3,5,7H2,1H3/t10-/m0/s1, and the corresponding InChIKey is SNICXCGAKADSCV-JTQLQIEISA-N. That key resolves through the InChIKey-to-MOL resolver to a V2000 connection table (PubChem CID 89594) whose counts line is ' 12 13  0  0  1  0  0  0  0  0999 V2000', i.e. declared 12 atoms and 13 bonds. Reading the atom block element column, the only elements present are N (2 atoms) and C (10 atoms). The separately computed molecular formula of the structure is C10H14N2. DERIVED reconciliation: the table's declared atom count (12) equals the formula's heavy-atom count (10 C + 2 N = 12), so they match. Hydrogen convention: the table has no explicit hydrogens (atom block lists only N and C symbols), so the 14 hydrogens of C10H14N2 are implicit/valence-filled. This molecule has one stereocentre (the pyrrolidine carbon bearing the pyridyl ring), and the table does mark it: the counts line chiral flag is 1 (the 5th field of ' 12 13  0  0  1 ...') and the bond block carries the stereo (wedge) bond '  3  7  1  1'; consistently, the InChI carries /t10-/m0/s1 and the InChIKey stereo block is JTQLQIEISA.

The InChIKey stereo block is UHFFFAOYSA (undefined stereo) instead of the defined block of the real (-)-menthol stereoisomer. The round trip is therefore stereochemically lossless only in the trivial sense that the stereo-free input is returned unchanged; the 3 stereocentres are represented as unspecified.

stereocentre_analysis.configuration_detail: The stereo-defining layers are byte-identical at every rung: /t2-/m0/s1 in the step-2 InChI, the step-4 InChI and the step-6 InChI, and the stereo block REOHCLBHSA in both InChIKeys (o003 and o007). evidence_from_returned_inchi.reading: The InChI carries an explicit double stereo layer: /t2- fixes the relative configuration at the atom numbered 2 in the canonical InChI numbering (the alpha carbon, bearing N, the CH2S group, the carboxyl carbon and H), and /m0 plus /s1 fix the absolute configuration. Exactly one atom number appears in the /t layer, so the InChI defines exactly one stereocentre.

evidence_from_returned_inchikey.reading: The second block of the InChIKey is the stereo/isotope block. The terminal letter S in ...BHSA codes the defined absolute configuration at the single stereocentre, matching the /t2-/m0/s1 layer. A single-centre, single-configuration signature is consistent with exactly one defined stereocentre (an undefined centre would leave the stereo block set to all-zeros style 'UHFFFAOYSA'-type indicator).

evidence_from_returned_structure.reading: The SMILES uses an explicit tetrahedral marker [C@@H] on one carbon only. That carbon is bonded to N (amino), the CH2S side chain, C(=O)O (carboxyl) and an implicit H: four different substituents, hence one defined tetrahedral stereocentre. No other atom in the molecule carries a stereo marker or can be a stereocentre.

stereocentre_analysis.analysis: Valine is (2S)-2-amino-3-methylbutanoic acid. The alpha carbon C2 is bonded to NH2, COOH, isopropyl and H: four different substituents, so it is defined. The beta carbon C3 carries two equivalent methyl groups (C1 and C2 of the isopropyl), so it is NOT a stereocentre. The count is therefore 1, not 2 and not 0.

stereocentre_analysis.evidence_from_structure_notation: SMILES CC(C)[C@H](N)C(=O)O contains exactly one @ tetrahedral marker, on the alpha carbon; the two methyl groups are written as plain equivalent branches with no marker.
stereocentre_analysis.survival_evidence: The /t4-/m0/s1 layer is present and identical in the step-2, step-4 and step-6 InChIs, and the @ marker is present and identical in the step-1 and step-5 SMILES, so the single defined (S) configuration is preserved end to end.
